archetype.name: Playoff Team (puck-driving, power-play led)
archetype.definition: A team that wins on shot volume, a deep forward group and one of the league's best power plays, without a goaltending or blueline edge to make it a true contender.

report.headline: Vegas is winning on process, not luck, but needs more from the crease.
report.take:
Vegas sits 13-6-3, second in the Pacific behind Edmonton, and tenth on the site's Teams tab. The underlying profile backs the record. A Goal Diff / GP of 0.5 ranks 8th, the 5-on-5 xGF % of 52.9% also ranks 8th, and the team puts 29.5 shots a game on goal (4th) while allowing 25.7 (9th). It also isn't leaning on bounces: 5-on-5 PDO is 99.3, below average, and Pts vs Goal Diff of 1 is ordinary. This is a team outplaying people in a sustainable way.

The engine is up front. The forwards grade A-, and the scoring runs through Jack Eichel (27 points) and Mitch Marner (26), with Mark Stone (11 goals) and Tomas Hertl adding finish. Hertl is the most interesting line on the sheet: a 63.8% xGF on 15.74 minutes a night, less ice than William Karlsson gets for 8 points. The power play converts 28.8% (4th), and that isn't a hot streak. The 2024-25 team ran at 28.3%, so this unit has done it before.

The weak spots are behind the forwards. The blueline and the goaltending both grade C+. Rasmus Andersson is a -9 with a sub-50% xGF on more than 19 minutes a night, and Jeremy Lauzon has a single point on over 17 minutes. In net, the split is clear. Adin Hill has a .908 save % and +3.6 GSAx over 10 starts, while Carter Hart has taken 12 starts at .888 and -1.1. Team GSAx of 1.2 is league-average, a real improvement on last season's -16.5, but it is not yet a strength. The penalty kill (76.8%, 18th) completes the picture of an average defensive structure.

The recent trend is mixed. The last 10 games went 5-2-3, a points pace close to the season's, but scoring fell 0.56 goals a game below the season rate and the differential nearly flattened. Three overtime losses and a 6-3 home loss to last-place Vancouver are the kind of slippage to watch. The shot volume says the goals should return; Marner's 3 goals on 48 shots and Karlsson's 3 on 41 point to finishing that is due to improve. Expect a comfortable playoff team that rises or falls with which goalie gets the net.

strengths.title: Shot volume and chance share
strengths.body: Vegas is 4th in shots on goal a game and 8th in 5-on-5 xGF %, while allowing fewer shots than most. The deep forward group carries play: Barbashev, Connelly and Hertl are all well above 58% xGF. A 5-on-5 PDO below 100 means this is not inflated by luck, so it should hold.

strengths.title: An elite, repeatable power play
strengths.body: At 28.8% the power play ranks 4th and sits well above the league's 22.2%. Eichel, Stone and Marner each have 11 or 12 PP Points. It matches the 2024-25 rate, so it looks like a structural edge rather than a run of good fortune.

strengths.title: Forward depth beyond the stars
strengths.body: The A- forward grade isn't one player carrying the group. Hertl (10th among centers) drives play at 63.8% xGF on middle-six minutes, and Connelly has 7 goals as a young third-line wing. That depth lets Vegas outshoot teams even when the top line is quiet.

concerns.title: Goaltending split favors the backup
concerns.body: Hart has made the most starts but sits at .888 with negative GSAx, while Hill is at .908 and +3.6. The team total is merely average after last season's -16.5 collapse. Unless the starts tilt toward Hill or Hart improves, the C+ grade caps the ceiling.

concerns.title: Thin blueline below the top pair
concerns.body: Theodore and McNabb are solid, both near 58% xGF, but Andersson is -9 with a 47.8% xGF on heavy minutes. Lauzon has 1 point on more than 17 minutes a night. The C+ grade and a middling penalty kill reflect a defense that relies on the forwards holding the puck.

concerns.title: Scoring has cooled lately
concerns.body: Over the last 10, Vegas scored 0.56 goals a game below its season rate, and the differential shrank to +1. Three of those 10 games went to overtime and were lost. The shot volume suggests this is finishing noise rather than decline, but it has cost points.

trend.note: An 8-6 October and a 4-3 November, with a last-10 points pace almost identical to the season's. The underlying play is stable, even if goals have dipped of late.

weekAhead.headline: Two home tests against Dallas, then a soft Winnipeg defense
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with back-to-back home games against Dallas, 7th on the site and a defense-first team. Dallas ranks 3rd in goals against, 3rd in shots allowed and 3rd on the penalty kill, behind A-graded goaltending. That is a direct collision with Vegas's two best weapons, shot volume and the power play. The Stars' offense is only 23rd, so these should be low-event games where Vegas's goalie choice matters.

The trip to Winnipeg is the opposite. The Jets allow the most shots in the league, their goalies are 27th in save %, their kill is 24th, and they give up points to defensemen at one of the worst rates in the league. A split with Dallas and a win in Winnipeg would be a solid week.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas power play vs Dallas kill
keyMatchups.body: Vegas's 4th-ranked power play meets a Dallas kill at 88.4%, 3rd in the league. Whichever unit wins this likely decides at least one of the two games, given how few goals Dallas allows.

keyMatchups.title: Wingers against a stingy Dallas
keyMatchups.body: Dallas holds wingers under expectation (5th) and concedes an unusually small share of its points to them, while centers take a large share. That tilts the burden toward Eichel and Hertl rather than Stone and Marner.

keyMatchups.title: Volume against leaky Winnipeg
keyMatchups.body: Winnipeg allows 32 shots a game (last in the league) with a .881 save %. That is the ideal setting for a team that shoots as much as Vegas, and a natural spot for slumping finishers to break out.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts the Dallas games: Hill's numbers make him the better bet in tight, low-scoring games.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable: an above-average chance share, top-five shot volume and a power play with a track record. None of it depends on luck, because 5-on-5 PDO is below 100 and the close-game ledger is roughly neutral. If anything, the forwards should finish better as Marner's and Karlsson's shooting comes back. The current 108-point pace is a reasonable top end, but an average penalty kill and a goaltending split that hasn't settled argue for a slightly lower landing spot, somewhere around 100 to 106 points.

The gap to Edmonton in the division is real, but the playoffs look safe. What separates a second-round team from a deeper run is the crease. A Hill-heavy workload close to his current form would push this toward the 2024-25 version of the team; more Hart starts at his current level would pull it back toward last season's goaltending problems.
swingFactors: Split of starts between Hill and Hart
Second-pair defense and the penalty kill

confidence.note: 22 games: the shot and chance metrics are stable, while goalie save rates are still noisy.
